CausalChain: Targeted gut microbiome modulation (via probiotics/FMT) -> Enhanced conversion of primary bile acids to higher UDCA and lower DCA levels -> Shift in bile acid receptor activation (FXR, TGR5, PXR) -> Downstream signaling modulation (reduced NF-kB, enhanced apoptosis and anti-inflammatory pathways, inhibited EMT) -> Inhibition of proliferation and decrease in cancer stem cell maintenance in colonic epithelium -> Reduced colorectal cancer risk
Hypothesis: Modulating the gut microbiome through targeted interventions such as strain-specific probiotics, prebiotics, or fecal microbiota transplantation, in combination with nanodelivery systems for bile acid receptor modulators, will promote the gut microbial conversion of primary bile acids into a favorable bile acid profile (characterized by increased UDCA and decreased DCA). This alteration is expected to preferentially activate anti-tumorigenic bile acid receptors (FXR, TGR5, PXR), leading to downstream suppression of NF-kB mediated inflammatory pathways, enhancement of apoptotic and anti-inflammatory signaling, and inhibition of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and cancer stem cell maintenance. Comprehensive multi-omics analyses will be employed to precisely quantify these molecular changes, thereby demonstrating a direct mechanistic link to a reduced risk of colorectal cancer.
Abstract: We propose that targeted modulation of the gut microbiome—achieved via specific probiotics, prebiotics, or fecal microbiota transplantation, integrated with advanced nanodelivery systems—to favor the microbial conversion of primary bile acids into the tumor‐suppressive ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) while limiting production of the pro‐carcinogenic deoxycholic acid (DCA), will shift bile acid receptor activation in colonic tissues toward anti-proliferative and anti-inflammatory pathways. This refined hypothesis incorporates multi-omics approaches (metabolomics, transcriptomics, metagenomics) to quantitatively assess the shift in bile acid profiles and receptor-mediated signaling (via FXR, TGR5, and PXR) that ultimately lead to suppressed NF-kB activation, enhanced apoptotic signaling, inhibited epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and reduction in cancer stem cell maintenance. Through this integrated strategy, we aim to provide a novel, technologically mature framework for colorectal cancer prevention.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused on modulating the gut microbiome to alter bile acid conversion (increasing UDCA while reducing DCA) to shift bile acid receptor activation toward anti-proliferative and anti-inflammatory effects, reducing colorectal cancer risk. In the revised hypothesis, we have expanded the concept by specifying practical intervention strategies (e.g., targeted probiotics, prebiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation) and incorporating contemporary technological capabilities such as nanodelivery systems and multi-omics profiling. Each step of the original causal chain has been explicitly retained: (1) microbiome modulation leading to differential bile acid conversion, (2) altered UDCA/DCA ratios affecting receptor activation (FXR, TGR5, PXR), (3) resulting in modulation of signaling pathways (reduced NF-kB, enhanced apoptosis and anti-inflammatory signaling, inhibited EMT), (4) ultimately leading to inhibition of proliferation and cancer stem cell maintenance. These refinements address prior gaps by specifying intervention methods, experimental approaches, and the use of modern analytical tools to provide a more quantifiable and mechanistically robust framework for colorectal cancer prevention.
